name: Archive Frictions
description:
Join us for the opening of Archive Frictions, a Gallery-on-Demand exhibition at the Sasken Multimedia Gallery. The exhibition will be inaugurated with a public symposium exploring women’s work and presence through photographic archives.

At the heart of Archive Frictions is a remarkable archive of photographs discovered by PhD researcher Alexandra Gow at the National Galleries Scotland. Believed to have been taken in the Indian subcontinent in the early to mid-1900s, the photographs offer a unique glimpse of women in university settings. In contrast to many stereotypical representations of India from the period, these images focus on women in educational spaces and are marked by an unusually intimate photographic style.

Two contemporary artists — Priyadarshini Ravichandran, based in India, and Steffi Klenz, based in the UK, have responded to the archive through the creation of new visual works. In doing so, Archive Frictions fosters a dynamic dialogue between historical and contemporary perspectives, illuminating the evolving representation of women in photography across time and cultural contexts.

 

Please find more details about the symposium and launch below:

Date: September 13, 2026

Time: 03:00 - 06:30 PM

Schedule:

03:00 - 03:30 PM: An Introduction to Fast Forward & Archive Frictions by Anna Fox

03:30 - 04:00 PM: Launch and walkthrough of Archive Frictions 

04:30 - 05:15 PM: Presentation by Suryanandini Narain

This talk will discuss two photographic albums by Mary Louisa Booth (1896-1939), titled the Antiquities of Kathiawad (c. 1910) and The Watson Memorial Institute, Rajkot (1893). Together, the albums are testament to the Raj’s interest in India’s pre-colonial archaeology, as well as its civic modernisation under the guidance of the British government. Mary Louisa Booth’s albums possibly make her the first woman photographer in the field of Indian archaeology.

05:30 - 06:30 PM: Archive Frictions: Contemporary Interpretations

This discussion will feature artists Priyadarshini Ravichandran and Steffi Klenz in conversation with Mira Brunner regarding their creative responses to the archive and their practices at large.

 

About the speakers:

Anna Fox is an acclaimed British photographer and Professor of Photography at the University for the Creative Arts. Working in colour, Fox first gained attention for Work Stations: Office Life in London (1988), a study of office culture in Thatcher’s Britain. She is best known for Zwarte Piet (1993-8), a series of portraits taken over five years that explore Dutch black-face folk traditions associated with Christmas. Fox is currently working on the research project Fast Forward: Women in Photography, for which she has been awarded a Leverhulme International Networks Grant, an AHRC Engagement Fellowship and an AHRC Follow on Award, as well as being supported in China, the UK, Nigeria and India by the British Council. 

Suryanandini Narain is Assistant Professor in Visual Studies at the School of Arts and Aesthetics, Jawaharlal Nehru University. Her research and critical writing focus on photography, visual culture and aesthetics. Her recent scholarly work includes co-editing Framing Portraits, Binding Albums: Family Photographs in India (Zubaan, 2024). 

Steffi Klenz is a London-based artist who approaches photography as an expanded visual discipline. Her work has been exhibited widely across the UK, including at the Royal Academy, the British Museum, the Wellcome Collection and Camden Art Centre in London, and the Royal Scottish Academy in Edinburgh. Internationally, her work has been shown at the Museum of Contemporary Art Taipei, the Finnish Museum of Photography in Helsinki, Künstlerhaus Bethanien in Berlin, CICA Museum in South Korea and FotoMuseum Antwerp. She has participated in major international exhibitions and festivals, including the British Council exhibition presented alongside Documenta in Athens (2017), the Biennale for Contemporary Photography in Germany (2020), the International Biennale for Photography in Belo Horizonte (2021), the Tokyo Biennale (2023), Bodø European Capital of Culture (2024) and the International Biennale of Contemporary Art in Uzbekistan (2024).

Priyadarshini Ravichandran is a photographer from Tamil Nadu working closely with recurrent themes emerging in relationships that root, reveal or unsettle her. She is compelled to tell stories of women, our lives and the land. She seeks to collaborate with researchers, friends, institutions, trees and animals- placing her in unexpected intersections. She received the Parasol Prize from the V&A Museum (2023) and the Quai Branly Museum award(2024).

Mira Brunner is a Bengaluru-based artist, archivist, and writer. She works across media, is interested in deep time and epistemology, and is informed by queer & disability studies. She has exhibited her work at the Museum of Art and Photography, Bengaluru (2026), 24 Hours Neukölln, Berlin (2026), the Chennai Photo Biennale, Chennai, (2025), neunKelche e.V., Berlin (2024), Dekalb Gallery, Brooklyn (2024), and University of the Arts, London (2023). Her writing has been published in Lassitude Zine, Sick Magazine, The Asian Journal of Women’s Studies, and Out of Print Magazine. On weekdays, she’s the chief archivist at QAMRA – the Queer Archive for Memory, Reflection, and Activism.

 

Archive Frictions is delivered in collaboration between Museum of Art and Photography (MAP), in Bengaluru, the National Galleries Scotland (NGS), in Edinburgh, and Fast Forward: Women in Photography. It is supported by the University of Creative Arts and British Council.

name: How Objects Become Icons: Photography, Publishing and the Making of Design History
description:
Studio Ballo+Ballo, 1954, Divano D70, Osvaldo Borsani for Tecno
Join us for a talk with historian and curator Libby Sellers exploring how twentieth-century design became iconic not simply through the objects themselves, but through the visual ecosystems that surrounded them: photography, magazines, catalogues, advertising, exhibitions, museums and collecting. 

Beginning with John Berger’s Ways of Seeing and the idea that every image embodies a particular way of seeing, the talk considers how images have shaped our understanding of what design looks like, what it means, and which objects and designers become part of the cultural canon.

From post-war Italian design through Californian architecture, it asks how photography transforms both the built environment and our understanding of it. The talk then brings this framework into a South Asian context through the architect Minnette de Silva and the journal MARG, exploring the role of publishing in making a regional modernism visible and intelligible, while opening questions around gender, authorship and the construction of the design canon. Drawing on research into twentieth-century furniture, women designers and collectible design, the talk asks who gets photographed, published, collected and remembered, and who remains outside the frame. 

Ultimately, the talk asks: when we think we recognise an iconic object, are we recognising the object itself, or the history of images that has taught us how to see it?

name: The Universe
description:
What if the artworks in a museum's collection became the building blocks of your own universe? In this session designed by Abhishek Lamba, a single deck of cards unlocks three different games — each one inviting you to draw on works from the collection, and use them as material for chance, strategy, and imagination. Come play, build, and see the collection in a way you never have before.

This event is part of Plural Worlds, developed in collaboration with Lagori Collective and presented in conjunction with Beneath the Turning Sky.

name: Reading the Film Poster
description:
What can a film poster reveal when we take the time to really look at it?

Facilitated by Rajesh Devraj and Ashish Rajadhyaksha, this intimate, off-the-cuff session invites participants to gather around a table and closely examine a selection of film posters, unpacking the many layers contained within each image. Through conversation and collective looking, we’ll explore the artistic styles, printing techniques, regional variations, typography, visual conventions and business strategies that shaped these objects—and the ways in which they communicated with audiences.

name: Making Art, Making Access
description:
What happens when we think about access in museums not simply as a question of entry, but as a question of how we experience, participate, navigate and belong?

Making Art, Making Access brings together artists, disabled practitioners, museum professionals, accessibility practitioners, researchers, designers and technologists for an afternoon of conversation, exchange and exploration.

Together, we will ask:

How do bodies, identities and lived experiences shape the ways we participate in cultural spaces?

How do design, technology, services, policy and research influence who can access and navigate museums?

What can museums do differently to create more meaningful and inclusive experiences?

The afternoon brings together artistic practice, disability scholarship, museum research and practical approaches to accessibility. Participants will also have an opportunity to engage with research emerging from MAP’s work on museum accessibility and technology, offering insights into audience needs, existing gaps and possibilities for action.

More than a series of talks, the mixer is an opportunity to meet like-minded people, exchange ideas and build connections across art, culture, accessibility, technology and design.

Making Art, Making Access is part of MAP’s ongoing work to learn, experiment and rethink what accessibility can look like in museums - and an invitation to imagine those possibilities together.

 

Please find the programme below:

2:00 – 2:10 PM: Welcome & Setting the Context
MAP 

An introduction to the afternoon and the central question: How can artists and museums adopt technology to create more accessible ways of experiencing art?

2:10 – 2:45 PM: Artist-led Keynote by Akhila Vimal C.

A practice-led exploration of technology, adaptation and artistic practice, and how these can challenge conventional ideas of how art is created, experienced and accessed.

2:45 – 3:00 PM: Pause & Reset

A short, participatory pause to refresh, reset and reconnect before the next session.

3:00 – 3:45 PM: Museum Accessibility Practices : A map for MAP by Gaurav Raheja

Exploring the intersection of museums, information and communication design, technology, services, and legal and policy frameworks. 

Drawing on examples from museums around the world, the session will examine how these different systems come together to shape who can access, navigate and participate in cultural spaces—and what institutions can learn from emerging approaches to inclusive design and accessibility.

3:45 – 4:00 PM: Coffee / Tea Break

A short break and an opportunity for informal conversations and connections.

4:00 – 4:45 PM: From Possibility to Practice by Mudito

Drawing on Mudito’s accessibility and technology research with MAP, this session explores audience needs, existing gaps and opportunities, and how museums can translate accessibility and technology into practical institutional action.

4:45 – 5:00 PM: Pause & Reset

A short, participatory pause to refresh and reset before the final session.

5:00 – 5:45 PM: One Platform, Many Museums by Bloomberg Connects

An exploration of how shared digital infrastructure can help museums adopt technology, expand access to collections and exhibitions, and create more accessible pathways to interpretation and engagement.

5:45 – 6:15 PM: Closing: What Do We Take Forward? 

A closing reflection bringing together the afternoon’s conversations and identifying key learnings, potential collaborations and directions for MAP’s future work on accessibility and technology.

Who is this for?

The programme is intended for artists, museum and cultural professionals, accessibility practitioners, disabled people and disability organisations, technology and digital experience professionals, researchers, designers, educators and students interested in rethinking access to art and culture.

Join us for an afternoon of conversations, demonstrations, shared learning and new possibilities for making art and museums more accessible.

name: Counter Mapping: Local Realities
description:
We all carry maps of the places we know: the street we take home, the room we grew up in, the neighbourhoods we navigate every day. But what do these maps leave out? What might happen if we mapped not only buildings and roads, but also water, heat, birds, memories, labour, decay, waiting, migration, infrastructure, and imagined futures? What if a familiar place could be encountered as one that holds several worlds at once?
Facilitated by Ishita Jain from Living Midnight Narrative Outfit, participants will choose a familiar and intimate place and begin to map its invisible territories. Through drawing, tracing, layering, and juxtaposition, they will explore its environmental, biological, social, infrastructural, and temporal layers, while considering the futures that might already be latent within these relationships.
As the maps take shape, they may begin to move beyond conventional representations of place, becoming fields of movement, encounters, and possibilities. The aim is not to create a more accurate map of a familiar world, but to explore what becomes visible when the way of seeing it changes.

This event is part of Plural Worlds, developed in collaboration with Lagori Collective and presented in conjunction with Beneath the Turning Sky.

name: The Momentary and the Monumental - Publication Launch
description:
What can a lobby card tell us about the ways we have imagined, remembered and encountered Indian cinema?

Marking the launch of the publication ‘The Momentary and the Monumental’, this panel brings together contributors Ashish Rajadhyaksha, Debashree Mukherjee and Iyesha Geeth Abbas to reflect on the histories, aesthetics and material lives of popular cinema publicity. Moving beyond the films themselves, the conversation will consider lobby cards and related ephemera as carefully constructed visual objects—shaped by photographers, artists, designers, printers and the conditions of their circulation.

Drawing on their contributions to the publication, the speakers will explore what these often-overlooked images reveal about the visual language of Indian cinema, the cultures of print and publicity that surrounded it, and the ways in which cinematic memory is produced beyond the screen. The discussion will also open up questions around the archives and histories that remain to be uncovered, and what it means to look closely at the material traces of popular cinema.

name: Tracing Color
description:
Drawing from MAP’s textile collection, this workshop explores how textiles can carry memories through colour, material and repair. Using a curated selection of objects, including kantha, patchwork, appliqué, quilting, embroidered purses, shawls, saris and shade cards, participants will closely observe the traces of making, mending, wear and care embedded within each object.

Beginning with observation, participants will reflect on the personal associations these textiles evoke, whether it is a grandmother’s quilt, a mother’s sari, a well-worn shawl or a favourite piece of clothing. These memories become a starting point for developing a visual vocabulary of colours, marks and rhythms that responds to the material qualities of the objects rather than reproducing them.

Registration for the event will open soon!

This programme is exclusively for 18–25 year olds.

This session is conducted as part of our engagements for the MAP Youth Collective. The MAP Youth Collective is a community for young people (18-25 year olds) to engage with the arts and culture sector. The collective is for, of and by young people — to explore our shared identities and interests through art.
